# Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
source("R/skill_download.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

Cleaning is where an AI assistant looks most useful and where its mistakes are
hardest to see. A cleaning script can run without error, return the right
columns and produce plausible values while having treated a missing-value code
as a measurement, kept the same animal twice, or dropped a row nobody noticed.
None of these raises an error.

This block treats cleaning as four artefacts, each with a different owner:

| Artefact | Owner | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Codebook (`docs/codebook.csv`) | You | Missing-value codes, units, valid ranges and label mappings are facts about how the data were collected. They cannot be inferred reliably from the values. |
| Cleaning skill | Reusable | *How* you clean: never touch raw data, log every change, never drop a row silently. The same for every dataset. |
| Validation and audit scripts | You, or a separate AI conversation | Written from the codebook, independently of the cleaning code, so one misunderstanding cannot pass both. |
| Enforcement | Configuration | Rules that hold whether or not the agent follows its instructions. |

The `r glossary("codebook")` is the hub. The cleaning and the checks both read
it, but neither reads the other, so a misunderstanding in one is caught by the
other:

You will work on a version of the voles data with errors planted in it. Your
instructor holds the answer key, so at the end you can measure what your
pipeline caught and what it missed.

*⏱ ~54 minutes*

:::{.callout-note}
**Why not simply ask the AI to clean the data?** In a 2025 study, language
models given deliberately polluted tables found missing values in standard
formats but struggled with codes such as `-1` (a
`r glossary("sentinel value")`), rarely detected non-exact duplicates, and did
worse as errors increased (Spreafico et al., 2025). The models were older than
those you will use and did not write or run code, so treat this as a map of
where to look. Those error classes are planted in this block's data.
:::

## Step 0: Lock the raw data

Everything later depends on the raw file being exactly what the data provider
sent. The deny rules from [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) already protect
it; here you add a `r glossary("checksum")` and confirm the rules work.

**1. Record a checksum and commit it.** Run this once, yourself.

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
raw_path <- here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")
checksum_path <- here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")
writeLines(unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)), checksum_path)
```

Then commit `tests/fixtures/raw_checksum.txt`.

**2. Confirm the deny rules are active.** In Claude Code, run `/permissions`.
The rules from `.claude/settings.json` should be listed, including the
`r glossary("deny rule")` `Edit(/data/raw/**)`.

**3. Test the control, do not assume it.** Ask:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Add a comment line to the top of data/raw/voles_raw.csv.
```

It should be refused. Then confirm the file is unchanged.

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
identical(unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)), readLines(checksum_path))
```

R returns `TRUE`. (The full test file in Step 5 also checks this, but its other
tests need the cleaned data, which do not exist yet.)

The deny rule prevents one route; the checksum detects a change made by any
route. *Going further* lists the full settings file and what each control
covers.


## Step 1: Profile the raw data (R, not AI)

Profiling is counting, and counting is something you should compute rather
than ask a model to estimate. Run the provided script yourself, in the R
console or with `Rscript scripts/00_profile.R` in the terminal:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# scripts/00_profile.R ----
# Purpose: describe the raw file as entered, before any decision is made.
# Every column is read as character so codes such as 9999 or -1 appear
# exactly as entered.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

raw_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# one row per column: missingness, distinct values, numeric range ----
profile_df <- raw_df |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |>
  # suppressWarnings: text values become NA here by design
  mutate(value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))) |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    n_distinct = n_distinct(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_numeric = sum(!is.na(value_num)),
    min_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else min(value_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else max(value_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = column
  )

# every distinct label in the categorical columns ----
labels_df <- raw_df |>
  select(sex, treatment_arm) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |>
  count(column, value, sort = TRUE)

# identifiers that appear more than once ----
repeated_ids_df <- raw_df |>
  count(subject_id) |>
  filter(n > 1)

print(profile_df, n = Inf)
print(labels_df, n = Inf)
print(repeated_ids_df)
```

Keep the output. It is the factual input to Step 2.


## Step 2: Draft the codebook, then audit it

The codebook is the data dictionary you wrote for the README on Day 2
([Fixing it with structure, cleaning and a README](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-fix)),
with machine-readable rules added: valid ranges, missing-value codes and label
mappings that both the cleaning skill and the validation rules can read.

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Draft and audit the codebook (12 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**1. Let an AI draft it from the profile alone.** Use a browser chat window,
not Claude Code: started in your workshop repository, Claude Code could open
`docs/data_note.md` itself, and the point of this step is to see what the AI
infers without it. Paste only the profile output.

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
Here is a profile of a raw data file. Draft a codebook as CSV with the
columns: column, type, rule, min, max, missing_codes, unit, source.
In the source column, state for every entry whether it comes from the
profile or is your assumption.

[paste the output of scripts/00_profile.R]
```

Save the draft as `docs/codebook.csv` yourself. The deny rules stop the agent
from writing that file: the codebook is yours.

**2. Audit the draft.** Before you open `docs/data_note.md`, answer:

- Did the draft list `9999` as a missing-value code, or treat it as a large
  measurement?
- Did it notice that `-1` is a code?
- Where did its `min` and `max` come from? A range read off the data includes
  the errors in the data, so it cannot be used to detect them. Valid ranges
  must come from the biology or the protocol.

**3. Correct it against the data provider's note.** Open `docs/data_note.md`
and edit the codebook yourself. Every line should be traceable to the note or
to a decision you can defend. Commit it.

::::
:::

`r hide("A codebook you could converge on")`

```
column,type,rule,min,max,missing_codes,unit,source
subject_id,character,"pattern ^V[0-9]{3}$; unique; pad digits to three",,,,,data note
sex,character,"allowed M, F; recode male to M, female to F",,,,,data note
treatment_arm,character,"allowed Control, Low_dose, High_dose; match case-insensitively",,,,,data note
mass_pre_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records)
mass_post_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records)
metabolic_rate_post,double,,5,30,-1,<unit>,data note (range from equipment)
```

## Step 3: Run the validation rules

Validation rules are transcribed from the codebook, not from the cleaning
script. If the same AI conversation writes both, a single misunderstanding (for
example, that `-1` is a valid reading) passes both.

The template provides `scripts/functions/validate_voles.R`, written from the
codebook by a person. It uses the pointblank package: each line is one rule,
and `interrogate()` reports how many rows break it. (pointblank calls the
object that holds the rules an "agent"; it has nothing to do with AI agents.)
You do not need to write pointblank code today.

`r hide("The provided version")`

```{r}
#| eval: false
# scripts/functions/validate_voles.R ----
# Rules transcribed from docs/codebook.csv by a human, not by the agent
# that writes the cleaning script.

voles_col_types <- function() {
  readr::cols(
    subject_id = readr::col_character(),
    sex = readr::col_character(),
    treatment_arm = readr::col_character(),
    mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(),
    mass_post_g = readr::col_double(),
    metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(),
    .default = readr::col_character()
  )
}

validate_voles <- function(data, label) {
  data |>
    pointblank::create_agent(label = label) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_not_null(columns = c(subject_id, sex, treatment_arm)) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_regex(columns = subject_id, regex = "^V[0-9]{3}$") |>
    pointblank::rows_distinct(columns = subject_id) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_in_set(columns = sex, set = c("M", "F")) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_in_set(
      columns = treatment_arm,
      set = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")
    ) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_between(
      columns = c(mass_pre_g, mass_post_g),
      left = 15, right = 60, na_pass = TRUE
    ) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_between(
      columns = metabolic_rate_post,
      left = 5, right = 30, na_pass = TRUE
    ) |>
    pointblank::interrogate()
}
```

`r unhide()`

**Run the rules on the raw data. They should fail.** If raw data pass every
rule, either the data are already clean or the rules are too weak, and you
should suspect the second. Run the provided `scripts/02_validate.R` in the R
console:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# scripts/02_validate.R ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

raw_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types())
validate_voles(raw_df, "Raw data: expected to FAIL")
```

Note which rules fail and how many rows each flags. Every failure is a problem
that the cleaning must resolve or log.

:::{.callout-warning}
`na_pass = TRUE` lets genuine missing values through. It would also let
through a cleaning script that replaced *every* mass with `NA`. Validation
alone cannot catch over-cleaning; the audit in Step 5 can.
:::

## Step 5: Check the result

Five checks, each catching something the others cannot.

**1. Validation on clean data should pass.**

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))
clean_df <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"),
  col_types = voles_col_types()
)
validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data: expected to pass")
```

**2. The tests: raw data unchanged and every row accounted for.** The provided
`tests/test_cleaning.R`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# tests/test_cleaning.R ----
library(testthat)
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

read_chr <- function(...) {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here(...),
    col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())
  )
}

test_that("raw data are unchanged", {
  recorded <- readLines(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt"))
  current <- unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")))
  expect_identical(current, recorded)
})

test_that("every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log", {
  raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")
  clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
  excluded_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv")

  expect_equal(nrow(raw_df), nrow(clean_df) + nrow(excluded_df))
  expect_setequal(
    c(clean_df$raw_row, excluded_df$raw_row),
    as.character(seq_len(nrow(raw_df)))
  )
  expect_false(any(is.na(excluded_df$reason) | excluded_df$reason == ""))
})

test_that("clean data pass every codebook rule", {
  clean_df <- readr::read_csv(
    here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"),
    col_types = voles_col_types()
  )
  validation <- validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data")
  expect_true(pointblank::all_passed(validation))
})
```

In the R console, run
`testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_cleaning.R"))`.

**3. Audit the logs against the data.** The cleaning log was written by the
agent, so check it rather than trust it. Run the provided
`scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R` in the R console:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

to_long <- function(data, value_name) {
  data |>
    pivot_longer(
      -raw_row,
      names_to = "column",
      values_to = value_name,
      values_transform = as.character
    )
}

raw_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |>
  mutate(raw_row = as.character(row_number())) |>
  to_long("raw_value")

clean_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |>
  to_long("clean_value")

cleaning_log_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# 1. Truthful: every logged old value matches the raw file ----
untruthful_df <- cleaning_log_df |>
  left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
  filter(!map2_lgl(old_value, raw_value, identical))

# 2. Complete: every changed cell appears in the log ----
unlogged_df <- clean_long_df |>
  left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
  filter(!map2_lgl(clean_value, raw_value, identical)) |>
  anti_join(cleaning_log_df, by = c("raw_row", "column"))

untruthful_df
unlogged_df

# 3. What kinds of change were made ----
cleaning_log_df |> count(column, rule, sort = TRUE)

# 4. Ten logged changes to check by hand against the raw file ----
set.seed(2026)
cleaning_log_df |> slice_sample(n = 10)
```

`untruthful_df` and `unlogged_df` should both have zero rows. An unlogged
change is the most dangerous outcome in this block: a value altered with no
record. If a row appears, inspect it; a difference in number formatting is
harmless, a changed value is not. For the ten sampled changes, open the raw file
yourself and confirm each one.

**4. Reproduce it without the agent.** Your `AGENTS.md` and the skill asked for
a script that runs in a `r glossary("fresh R session")` with the packages in
the `r glossary("lockfile")`, `renv.lock`. Check, rather than trust. Commit the
outputs, then:

**In the terminal:**

```bash
Rscript -e "renv::status()"
Rscript scripts/01_clean.R
git status --short data/derived
```

`renv::status()` should report that the project is in a consistent state. If
the agent installed or used a package that is not in `renv.lock`, it says so;
decide whether you want the package, then update the lockfile with
`renv::snapshot()` as on [Day 1](01-projects.qmd). `Rscript` runs the script in
a fresh R session, and the same script on the same raw data must write the same
outputs, so `git status` should show no changes. If a derived file changed, the
cleaning is not deterministic: find out why before going on.

**5. Grade the pipeline against the planted errors.** Your instructor will now
release the answer key. For each planted error, record:

| Planted error | Failed validation on raw? | Handled as intended? | In the log? |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

The first column measures your *rules*; the second measures the *cleaning*;
the third measures the *record*. A planted error that passed validation on raw
data is a hole in your codebook, whatever the cleaning did.


## Debrief

1. Which planted errors did the AI's first draft of the codebook miss before you
   gave it the data provider's note? What does that say about who should own the
   codebook?
2. What did the agent do with the mass recorded in kilograms and the value ten
   times too large? If it "corrected" them, on whose authority? If the provider
   confirms a kilogram entry, the correction becomes a codebook rule you add,
   not something the script infers.
3. Which of your checks would have caught a script that set every mass to `NA`?

**Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you
automate this again?


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **Check:** validation rules transcribed from the codebook, not from the
  cleaning code; tests; the log audited against the raw file; the answer key.
- **Reproduce:** `renv::status()` and a fresh `Rscript` run that writes
  identical outputs. Once the clean output is right, you can freeze it as a
  reference, as you will in [Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd), so a
  later refactor of `01_clean.R` must reproduce it exactly.
- **Record:** the codebook, the cleaning and exclusion logs, and a line in
  `docs/ai-log.md`: the skill, how many planted errors were handled as
  intended, and anything you overrode.
:::


## Check your understanding

**Why must the codebook be written or confirmed by the analyst rather than
inferred by the AI from the data?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Because AI tools cannot read CSV files",
  answer = "Because missing-value codes, units and valid ranges are facts about how the data were collected; ranges read off the data include the very errors they are meant to detect",
  "Because codebooks must be written in a specific file format",
  "Because the AI would take too long to profile the data"
))`

**Your validation rules all pass on the raw data before any cleaning. What is
the most likely explanation in this exercise?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The cleaning script has already run",
  "pointblank cannot read raw data",
  answer = "The rules have gaps, because the raw data are known to contain errors",
  "The data are clean and no cleaning is needed"
))`

**How does the checksum test differ from the deny rule?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "They are equivalent; one is redundant",
  answer = "The deny rule blocks one route (the agent's editing tools) before a change happens; the checksum detects a change by any route, after it happens",
  "The checksum prevents edits; the deny rule only reports them",
  "The deny rule works on GitHub; the checksum works only locally"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards
if it is useful to you.

### The Step 0 controls in full

**Line endings.** The template's `.gitattributes` contains this line, so git
does not convert line endings, which would change the checksum on Windows:

```
data/raw/** -text
```

**Deny rules.** This is the `.claude/settings.json` in your workshop
repository, the same file you read in [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd):

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}
```

A leading `/` anchors each pattern to the project root. The rules protect
specific files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write
`scripts/01_clean.R` and `data/derived/`. Posit Assistant has no documented
path rules for file edits; use the guard hook from the *Going further* section
of [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) instead.

:::{.callout-warning}
**What each control covers.** The deny rule blocks the agent's file-editing
tools, and shell output redirects such as `> file`. It does not cover R code
the agent runs: an R script that writes to `data/raw/` is a different route.
The checksum test catches a change made by *any* route, but only after the
fact. On the Copilot cloud agent, where you have no local permission file, the
checksum test running in CI plus branch protection is your control. Use both
where you can: one prevents, the other detects.
:::

**Data governance.** A deny rule on editing does not stop data reaching the
model provider; see [Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd).

### Write the validation rules independently

Instead of using the provided `validate_voles.R`, you can have the rules
written by an AI that has never seen the cleaning code, for example a browser
chat window given only the codebook:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
Using only the codebook below, write an R file containing a function
validate_voles(data, label) that builds a pointblank agent with one
validation step per codebook rule, and interrogates it. Also write
voles_col_types(), returning readr column types for the codebook columns,
with character as the default for anything else.

[paste docs/codebook.csv]
```

Compare what it writes with the provided version in Step 3. A rule it missed,
or a range it took from the data rather than the codebook, is the kind of
error the separate conversation is meant to expose.
